articleTitle: The DVB project-digital television for Europe
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on DVB (Digital Video Broadcasting): The Future for Television Broadcasting?) (Digest No.1995/142)
abstract: In Europe, the development of standards for digital video broadcasting (DVB), as well as the preparation of the introduction of services, is coordinated by the European project on digital video broadcasting ("DVB project"). This paper describes the project as well as some of the achievements reached so far. Techniques for the transmission of DVB signals via satellite have been devised as well as a specification for transmission of DVB signals via cable and (S)MATV networks. A standard describing service information, a common scrambling system and several other tasks have been finalized. At present the specification for the terrestrial transmission of DVB signals is being finalized.

articleTitle: Terrestrial TV systems and frequency planning
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on DVB (Digital Video Broadcasting): The Future for Television Broadcasting?) (Digest No.1995/142)
abstract: In July 1994 the UK Government announced a plan as many as 12 digital terrestrial television services. Digital transmission offers the possibility of new programme services, a route to widescreen and improved quality, multichannel sound, and the potential for enhancements such as interactivity. Digital television can be delivered into viewers' homes by a variety of bearers including satellite, terrestrial, cable, and terrestrial broadcasting. It is likely that in the digital era there will be a mixed economy of these delivery systems together with, perhaps, new delivery techniques such as ADSL and ATM networks. However, digital terrestrial broadcasting has a number of unique properties which, for some viewers and applications, make it the most suitable replacement technology for today's analogue broadcasting. These include service to portable or mobile sets (and other receivers which are not connected to roof-top aerials), ability to deliver regional and local programming, and the potential for universal coverage. Preliminary planning studies for digital terrestrial television networks in the UK indicate that both single frequency networks (SFNs) and multi-frequency networks (MFNs) will have a role to play in providing good coverage for an attractive package of national, regional, and local programme services.

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on DVB (Digital Video Broadcasting): The Future for Television Broadcasting?) (Digest No.1995/142)
abstract: Digital compression of audio and video information is a key technology to transmit television programs more efficiently than with analogue technology. To exploit the compression technology in a cost effective way, standards have been agreed by several bodies, such as MPEG and DVB. Based on these standards, digital television services are becoming available. This paper discusses the functionality of digital television receivers for satellite and cable, and some constraints for interactive applications in digital television receivers. Furthermore cost constraints for receivers are discussed, as well as conditions for future integration into TV sets; initially a digital television receiver will be a set top box.

articleTitle: The commercial prospects for digital video broadcasting
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on DVB (Digital Video Broadcasting): The Future for Television Broadcasting?) (Digest No.1995/142)
abstract: The evolution of video compression systems giving a picture quality at data rates of 2 Mbit/s at least as good as that received on the average domestic PAL television set or played back from a video recorder, created great interest and provided a strong market drive for broadcasters to implement a complete direct-to-home (DTH) satellite programme delivery infrastructure having a capacity in excess of 100 channels from a single satellite. For such a system, leading to a mass market of receivers for the public, standardisation of the technical specification was essential. This task was taken up by the digital video broadcasting (DVB) project in 1993 and the main standardisation work for satellite and cable delivery systems completed in 1994, with the result that DTH satellite receivers have just started mass production. The most important aspect in the evolution of DVB has been that it was market-led by the application to satellite delivery. The DVB project, however, has recognised the importance of also formulating the technical standards for cable delivery, for terrestrial delivery and for MMDS.

articleTitle: Digital video broadcasting on cable television media
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on DVB (Digital Video Broadcasting): The Future for Television Broadcasting?) (Digest No.1995/142)
abstract: During the last decade the application of digital video and audio technology in broadcasting has developed at a considerable pace and has already penetrated the production process in studios and the contribution and distribution of programmes on transmission networks. However, the full benefit of this progress is only obtained when the complete chain from studio to home is digital. The paper illustrates how the digital video broadcasting standard can be adapted to the needs of broadcasters using cable systems.
